month.title: Product discovery + business
month.theme: Find consequential problems, gather evidence, and reason about value and distribution before building.
month.mastery: Explain why a problem is worth solving using actual evidence.
month.checkpoint: A dossier on one opportunity with interviews, a sizing model, alternatives, a business-model hypothesis and the result of a cheap test.

weeks.title: Problem discovery
weeks.objective: Notice expensive problems in the world around you, and describe them without jumping to solutions.
learn: Problems vs solutions vs features
Where problems hide: workarounds, spreadsheets, WhatsApp groups, complaints, job posts
Frequency × severity × willingness to act
Observing without pitching
Your unfair advantages: design skill, industry access, Indian SMB context
Problem statements that are specific and testable
Keeping an opportunity log
practice: Log 10 observations in the Opportunity Lab this week, with no solutions allowed
Find 3 spreadsheets or WhatsApp workflows people use to run a business
Read 20 negative reviews of a popular SMB tool
Rewrite 3 vague problems as specific ones

build.title: 10 observations, 3 deep-dives
build.brief: Fill the Opportunity Lab with 10 real observations. Pick 3 and complete every field: who, frequency, workaround, cost, existing solutions, and why they fall short.

weeks.prove: Pick your strongest observation and defend it against 'nobody would pay for that' with evidence, not enthusiasm.
reflect: Which problem did you want to be real more than the evidence supported?
weeks.ship: Opportunity Lab entries summarised in a public, anonymised note.

tryFirst.task: Rewrite this as a specific, testable problem: 'Small businesses struggle with marketing.'
tryFirst.hint: Who exactly? Doing what? How often? What do they do today, and what does it cost them?
tryFirst.explanation: Vague problems can't be tested or solved. A good problem statement names a specific person, situation, frequency, current workaround and cost, and each part can be checked in an interview.
tryFirst.solution:
'Owners of single-location bakeries in tier-2 Indian cities spend 3–5 hours a week making festival and offer posts on Canva or WhatsApp, often post late or skip festivals, and believe they lose walk-in sales on peak days. Today they ask a nephew or reuse last year's design.'

Testable parts: who, hours per week, missed posts, belief about lost sales, current workaround.

weeks.title: User research
weeks.objective: Learn the truth from real people through conversations that don't lead the witness.
learn: The Mom Test: talk about their life, not your idea
Recruiting: who to talk to and how to reach them
Interview scripts: open questions about specific past events
Note-taking: verbatim vs interpretation
Synthesis: affinity mapping, patterns, contradictions
Ethics: consent, privacy, payment
Signals of real pain: workarounds, spend, urgency
practice: Write an interview script with zero leading questions
Do a practice interview with a friend and critique yourself
Recruit 5 people who have your top problem

build.title: 5 interviews + synthesis
build.brief: Interview 5 people about your top opportunity. Record the evidence in the Opportunity Lab (with consent) and synthesise it: patterns, quotes, surprises, and what changed your mind.

weeks.prove: Show where your interviews contradicted your assumptions, with quotes.
reflect: What did you hear that you didn't want to hear?
weeks.ship: Synthesis board and an anonymised findings note.

tryFirst.task: Fix these two questions: 'Would you use an app that automates your invoicing?' and 'Don't you hate chasing payments?'
tryFirst.hint: Ask about specific past behaviour, not hypothetical futures or your idea. Don't put the answer in the question.
tryFirst.explanation: People are kind about hypotheticals and agree with leading questions. Past behaviour is evidence: what they did last time, how long it took, what they spent, what they tried.
tryFirst.solution:
Instead of 'Would you use…?':
  'Walk me through the last time you sent an invoice. What happened after that?'
Instead of 'Don't you hate…?':
  'When did a payment last arrive late? What did you do about it?'
Follow-ups: 'How often does that happen?' · 'What have you tried?' · 'What did it cost you?'

weeks.title: Opportunity sizing
weeks.objective: Estimate whether a problem is big enough to matter, bottom-up, with stated assumptions.
learn: TAM / SAM / SOM, and why top-down numbers mislead
Bottom-up sizing: customers × price × frequency
Finding data: government statistics, industry reports, proxies
Assumptions as variables you can test
Sensitivity: which assumption matters most
Market timing: why now?
Small markets that are still great businesses
practice: Size your top opportunity bottom-up in a spreadsheet
Find 3 independent data sources for your customer count
Change each assumption by ±50% and see what moves

build.title: Sizing model
build.brief: A bottom-up sizing spreadsheet for your top opportunity, with sources, assumptions, sensitivity and a 'why now'. Update the opportunity's market and timing scores with notes.

weeks.prove: Defend your biggest assumption with a source, or admit it's a guess and design a test for it.
reflect: Which assumption carries the whole model?
weeks.ship: Sizing model (spreadsheet) plus a short memo.

tryFirst.task: Size, bottom-up, the market for a ₹499/month posting tool for Indian bakeries.
tryFirst.hint: How many bakeries are there? What fraction are reachable and digitally active? What fraction might pay? Multiply by price × 12.
tryFirst.explanation: Bottom-up sizing makes every assumption visible and testable. The point isn't precision; it's knowing which number matters most and how to check it.
tryFirst.solution:
Bakeries (organised + unorganised, estimate):  ~1,00,000   [source / assumption]
Active on WhatsApp/Instagram for business:     × 40% = 40,000
Would pay for posts (from interviews):          × 10% =  4,000
Revenue: 4,000 × ₹499 × 12 ≈ ₹2.4 crore a year

Biggest sensitivity: the 10% willingness to pay. Test it with a pre-sale.

weeks.title: Business models and distribution
weeks.objective: Decide who pays, for what, and how they'll find you, then test the cheapest version.
learn: Business models: subscription, usage, transaction, services, marketplace
Value metric: what the price scales with
Pricing in India: willingness to pay, UPI, GST basics
Distribution channels: direct, partners, content, communities, marketplaces
Unit economics (CAC, LTV, payback) as intuition, not a finance degree
Doing things that don't scale
Pre-sales and concierge tests
practice: Map how 3 SMB tools you know acquire their customers
Write 3 pricing hypotheses and how you'd test each
Estimate customer acquisition cost for one channel
Design a concierge test you could run in a week

build.title: Opportunity research dossier
build.brief: Bring it all together: problem, evidence, interviews, sizing, alternatives, business model, distribution plan, risks, and the result of one cheap test (pre-sale, waitlist or concierge).

weeks.prove: Mastery test: explain why this problem is worth solving, using actual evidence.
reflect: What would make you stop pursuing this opportunity?
weeks.ship: Dossier published (anonymised) in your portfolio repo.

tryFirst.task: Design a one-week test of whether bakery owners will pay ₹499 a month for done-for-you festival posts, without writing any software.
tryFirst.hint: Deliver the service by hand to a few customers. What would count as real commitment rather than polite interest?
tryFirst.explanation: A concierge test delivers the value manually, to learn whether people pay and what they actually need. Real commitment means money, time or reputational risk, not 'sounds great'.
tryFirst.solution:
1. Pick 15 bakeries from your interviews or neighbourhood.
2. Offer: 'Diwali posts for your shop, ready for WhatsApp: ₹499 for festival week, pay by UPI after you see the first post.'
3. Make the posts yourself (Figma + templates).
4. Success criterion, set in advance: at least 4 of 15 pay, and at least 2 ask about the next festival.
5. Record who paid, the objections, and what they asked you to change.

mastery.title: Why this problem is worth solving
mastery.challenge: Make the case to a sceptical reviewer that one problem in your Opportunity Lab is worth solving, using evidence you gathered yourself.
constraints: Evidence must be first-hand: interviews, observations, test results
criteria: A specific problem statement: who, situation, frequency, current workaround, cost
At least 5 interviews or observations cited
Bottom-up sizing with the key assumption identified
Existing solutions, and why they fall short, in users' own words
One cheap test run, with a success criterion set in advance and an honest result
States what would make you stop
